composition: Nominal composition Fe–9Al–10Mn–1C (wt%) — 9 wt% Al, 10 wt% Mn, 1 wt% C, Fe balance — lying within the tested composition ranges of the study (Al 9–12, Mn 10–20–30, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe bal.). Aluminium is the principal density-reducing and κ-carbide-forming element, while Mn and C are added as austenite stabilizers to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of the Fe–Al system; C at the 1 wt% level (versus 0.4 wt% in the sibling lower-carbon grade) raises the Al–C chemical driving force for κ-carbide precipitation.
conclusions: Within the study of austenite decomposition in Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steels, the hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-1C condition functions as the as-received reference state. Its 273 HV hardness is the highest of the three 9Al–xMn–1C compositions examined (273, 233 and 216 HV for 10, 20 and 30 wt% Mn) and it is the baseline against which all tempering-induced hardening is measured. Compared with the tempered states, this condition shows that the strong hardening of this composition is not intrinsic to the hot-rolled state but is produced by the subsequent γ transformations — most notably a 273 → 439 HV rise on 600 °C tempering (discontinuous precipitation giving narrow-spacing γ + κ lamellae), which the paper identifies as the best-performing microstructure, versus a more modest 273 → 356 HV on 800 °C tempering.
mechanisms: Hot-rolling at 1150 °C followed by water quenching fixes the as-received microstructure and defines a high-temperature (1150 °C) austenite-equilibrium state; because the austenite phase fraction changes strongly with temperature (CALPHAD diagram for 9Al-10Mn-1C), this frozen high-temperature state is thermodynamically off-equilibrium at lower service/tempering temperatures, providing the gradient that drives γ decomposition upon subsequent tempering — although the authors note this comparison is indicative/qualitative only.

The measured 273 HV of the hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-1C is the reference baseline used to quantify the hardening produced by the subsequent austenite decomposition reactions: 600 °C tempering raises it to 439 HV (discontinuous precipitation to γ + κ lamellae) and 800 °C tempering to 356 HV (cellular transformation + spinodal decomposition).

In the 9Al–xMn–1C series the as-received (hot-rolled) hardness decreases with increasing Mn content from 273 HV (10 Mn) to 233 HV (20 Mn) and 216 HV (30 Mn), indicating that Mn level (austenite stability and its effect on the matrix/phase balance) governs the hardness of the un-tempered state; the paper does not give a further mechanistic explanation for this trend.
microstructure: The paper provides no micrograph or morphological description of the as-hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-1C condition; the optical/SEM microstructures reported for this composition (discontinuous precipitation at 600 °C, cellular transformation plus spinodal decomposition at 800 °C) belong exclusively to the tempered samples and must not be attributed to this as-received state. The only compositional/thermodynamic information bearing on this state is the CALPHAD equilibrium phase-fraction diagram calculated for 9Al-10Mn-1C (phases FCC_A1, BCC_A2, KAPPA_E21), which shows austenite (FCC_A1) rising to about 1.00 mol near ~1000 °C and remaining the dominant phase at the 1150 °C rolling temperature before declining at higher temperature; the authors stress that this diagram is only an indicative, qualitative indication of the thermodynamic gradient in austenite stability, because the hot-rolled condition is not identical to the state during hot-rolling at 1150 °C.
processing: Route: (1) casting — the alloy was produced by vacuum induction melting in a 100 kW furnace under vacuum, giving 0.5 kg ingots; (2) hot-rolling — the ingot was hot-rolled at 1150 °C into 5 mm flat product; (3) cooling — the flat product was water-quenched. This hot-rolled + water-quenched condition defines the as-received state of the sample; no tempering was applied to this particular specimen (the 600 °C and 800 °C/30 min tempers described in the paper belong to the heat-treated counterparts of this composition).
properties: Mechanical: Vickers macro-hardness of 273 HV for the hot-rolled (as-received) condition (5 kg load, 5 indentations per sample, outliers excluded). This is the highest hot-rolled hardness among the 9Al–xMn–1C series, which falls with increasing Mn (273 HV at 10Mn, 233 HV at 20Mn, 216 HV at 30Mn), and it is the baseline from which the tempering responses are quantified (600 °C temper → 439 HV; 800 °C temper → 356 HV). No tensile, physical or chemical properties were reported for this condition. Characterisation performed on the samples includes optical microscopy of through-thickness embedded, ground and polished specimens (done separately for hot-rolled and heat-treated conditions), secondary-electron SEM imaging and SEM-EDS where selected microstructures were studied, and Vickers macro-hardness testing; hardness data were checked for consistency with Minitab18®.
summary: The as-received (hot-rolled) condition of the Fe–9Al–10Mn–1C lightweight steel, prepared by vacuum-induction casting, hot-rolling at 1150 °C to 5 mm flat product and water quenching. It is the reference/as-received state in a study of the austenite (γ) decomposition reactions of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels, against which the 600 °C and 800 °C tempering responses of the same composition are compared. Its measured Vickers macro-hardness of 273 HV is used throughout the paper as the hot-rolled baseline of 9Al-10Mn-1C.
unmapped: No micrograph or morphological description of the as-hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-1C condition is given in the paper; all reported microstructures (discontinuous precipitation at 600 °C; precipitation transformation; cellular transformation and spinodal decomposition at 800 °C) belong to the tempered samples and are not properties of this hot-rolled sample.
The 9Al-10Mn-1C composition lies within the tested composition ranges of Table 1: Al 9–12 wt%, Mn 10–20–30 wt%, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe balance.

The hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-1C hardness of 273 HV serves as the as-received reference/baseline in the tempering comparisons of Tables 2 (600 °C, 439 HV), 5 and 8 (800 °C, 356 HV) and Table 9 (600 °C, inter-lamellar spacing 'Narrow').

Minitab18® software was used to verify the consistency of the acquired hardness data (outliers excluded) and to plot data highlighting chemical-composition and process effects; this data-analysis step is not specific to the hot-rolled condition.
